title: Making Revisions Understandable: A Survey of Edit Intentions, Methods, and Applications
key_contributions: Comprehensive taxonomy of edit intentions in text revision
Distinguishes content edits from clarity/coherence/grammar/style edits
Shows the same surface pattern (e.g., deletion) can reflect different intentions
Surveys methods for intent prediction and applications
Demonstrates edit intent classification depends on context and purpose, not just text

edit_taxonomy.note: The survey reviews taxonomies ALONG four dimensions (structure, definitions/examples, application domains, data availability) rather than enumerating one canonical label set. The paper's illustrative lineage taxonomy is:
meaning_changing: VERIFICATION (correcting factual errors or adding citations)
edit_taxonomy.structure_convention: Most edit-intention taxonomies are tree-based, up to three levels; three-level ones separate meaning-preserving from meaning-changing, sometimes refining by discourse scope or edited object.

key_insight: Edit intentions provide a high-level abstraction OVER surface-level differences, capturing underlying goals such as content elaboration, factual correction, stylistic refinement, or structural reorganization. The same surface pattern (e.g., a deletion) can reflect different intentions: removing redundancy (SIMPLIFICATION) vs. removing a requirement (content change).
direct_implication_for_skill: The skill's change_type taxonomy (semantic_shift, scope_narrowed, scope_broadened, field_renamed, requirement_added, requirement_removed) sits at the surface-edit-action level, whereas this survey's framing puts intent one level above. The skill's 'interpretation' and 'worked_example' fields are the place where intent is expressed — this paper argues that level is where the real signal is. The survey also notes definition quality varies and categories are often overly broad, which is a caution for the skill's own label definitions.
potential_application: When the skill marks a change as 'uncertain', could leverage this taxonomy to ask: 'Is this a content edit (scope change) or a style edit (field rename)?' This could help resolve ambiguous classifications.
reading_notes: This is a survey paper; most useful for understanding the broader landscape of edit types. Helps explain why simple lexical diffs fail: they don't distinguish intent. Key insight: same surface pattern → different semantic meaning depending on intent.
